title: the day the whole people says sorry together
hook: the day the whole people says sorry together

segments.voice: Yesterday: hitbodedut, going off alone to talk out loud in your own words. Your line was talk to him out loud. Did you find five minutes to speak? Day sixteen.

It's the evening of the holiest day of the Jewish year, and the synagogue is fuller than it's been all year. People who haven't come since last autumn are here. Many are dressed in white. Some are wearing sneakers under their good clothes. Nobody has eaten since before sunset, and nobody will until the stars come out tomorrow night. Then a cantor begins a melody so old and so familiar that some people cry before a word is sung, and it's sung three times, each time a little louder. For the next twenty-five hours, a whole people will say sorry, together. Today: Yom Kippur.
screen: `THE FULLEST NIGHT OF THE YEAR.` → `WHITE CLOTHES, NO FOOD.` → `A MELODY SUNG THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Yom Kippur means the day of atonement. The Torah sets it on the tenth day of the seventh month, in the autumn, and tells the people to afflict their souls, which the rabbis understood as a fast. So for about twenty-five hours: no food, no water, no leather shoes, no washing for pleasure. Many wear white, like angels, some say, who don't need to eat. The evening begins with Kol Nidre, the melody from the start. And then the confessions. Here's what surprises people. They're in the plural. Not I have sinned. We have. One confession runs through the Hebrew alphabet, a sin for every letter, and everyone says every line, lightly tapping their chest, including lines about things they personally never did. The whole community stands together as one. Nobody is singled out, and nobody gets to pretend they're above it. But the day has a limit, and the rabbis wrote it down plainly. The Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones for what's between a person and God. For what's between you and another person, it doesn't, until you've made it right with them. So in the days before, Jews call each other, write, knock on doors, and ask forgiveness. The fast doesn't replace the phone call. In the afternoon, the book of Jonah is read, a story about a whole city that turns around and is given another chance. And as the sun goes down, the last service is called Neilah, the closing of the gates. The doors of the ark stay open, the room stands, and at nightfall one long blast of the ram's horn ends it. Then everybody goes home and eats.
screen: `THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` · `WE HAVE SINNED, NOT I.` · `THE FAST DOESN'T REPLACE THE CALL.` · `NEILAH — THE CLOSING OF THE GATES.` · then, large: `ONE LONG BLAST OF THE SHOFAR.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. Bring to mind one person you owe an apology, big or small, recent or old. Don't write the speech yet. Just picture their face, and picture the moment of saying it. Notice what makes it hard. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to make the call. The bell holds the time.
Yom Kippur. The day of atonement: twenty-five hours of fasting, confessing together, and closing gates. Sixteenth word.
Your line: you can start over. Today, send the apology you pictured, or take one step toward it. The rest can come later. Day sixteen.

howItsDone: On Yom Kippur Jews fast for about twenty-five hours, many wear white and no leather shoes, and spend much of the day in synagogue, from Kol Nidre in the evening to Neilah and the final shofar blast at nightfall; in the days before, many ask forgiveness of people they have wronged.

original.note: Hebrew: the day of atonement. the Torah calls it yom ha-kippurim.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Jewish day of fasting.
what it means: a whole people confessing together in the plural, and a limit: wrongs against people need those people.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 16 and 23 set the tenth of the seventh month; Mishnah Yoma 8:9 draws the line between sins against God and against another person.

sources.ref: Leviticus 16:29–31; 23:27–32 (the tenth day of the seventh month; afflict your souls)
Mishnah Yoma 8:1 (the five afflictions) and 8:9 (between person and person)
The Yom Kippur liturgy: Kol Nidre, the alphabetical confession (Ashamnu), Neilah
The book of Jonah (read on Yom Kippur afternoon)

notes: Kol Nidre is technically a legal formula annulling vows; the script mentions only its melody. A Keeper may want a line on what it says.
